land.text: 'the area of present-day Upper Normandy which Rollo had previously conquered', ceded by Charles the Simple under the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte

predecessors.note: The infobox also lists the Kingdom of Brittany as a predecessor: it gave up the Cotentin and Avranchin in 933 (ledger gain 933).

land.text: continental Normandy, which Cliopatria folds into its Norman England row from 1072 (that row's shape reaches lat 47.99 in France)

successors.note: The duchy did not end: the Duchy page has the dukes 'usually also kings of England' from 1066 to 1204 and continental Normandy conquered by Philip II in 1204, ceded in 1259. This dossier stops where Cliopatria hands the land to Norman England.

capitals.name: Rouen
capitals.note: Infobox 'Capital: Rouen'; Richard I's 'stronghold' (962) on the Richard I page. The page gives no change of capital.

correction.text: Upper Normandy, the lower Seine around Rouen and the Pays de Caux: Rollo's county from the 911 treaty

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's first Normandy shape begins in 922 but the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte is 911: Charles the Simple 'ceded the area of present-day Upper Normandy which Rollo had previously conquered'. The 922 shape (8,959 km2, lon 0.0-1.8, lat 49.25-50.25) stands for it. The page gives no area.
8,959 km2 for 922-925: Rollo's county, 'Upper Normandy' of the 911 treaty. The pages give no area; the shape sits well inside the modern Seine-Maritime and Eure (about 12,300 km2).
29,227 km2: 'Hiémois and Bessin were taken in 924' and King Radulf 'extended Rollo's county westward up to the river Vire, including the Bessin'; Cliopatria draws the extension two years late (926).

union.text: the land between the Sélune and the Couesnon, with Mont-Saint-Michel

correction.text: The 936 shape without the Sélune-Couesnon strip and Passais, which the Normans take in 1009-1020 and 1050

keyframe_review.note: 35,366 km2: 'the Cotentin and a part of Avranchin followed in 933' (Cliopatria 936). Two cells are too early: the shape holds Mont-Saint-Michel, which the page gives to the Normans only 'between 1009 and 1020' ('all the land between the rivers Sélune and Couesnon, including Mont Saint-Michel'), and Domfront and its Passais, which the Alençon page puts in Maine ('Domfront was then in Maine') until William 'completed these campaigns in 1050 by taking Passais'. Both come back by ledger gains.

union.text: the land between the Sélune and the Couesnon, with Mont-Saint-Michel

correction.text: The 990 shape without the Sélune-Couesnon strip (until 1020) and Passais (until 1050)

keyframe_review.note: 37,896 km2: the shape grows south to lat 47.99 (cells at Alençon, Bellême and Mortagne enter in 990); no page dates that growth. The Alençon page: 'During the tenth century, Alençon was a buffer state between Normandy and the Maine regions', the town 'had risen in support of the Count of Anjou' in 1049-1051 and 'Bellême was held directly from King Henry I'; these cells are left as drawn but unverified. Same two early cells as 936: the Sélune-Couesnon strip (1009-1020) and Passais (1050) are removed until the ledger gains.

39,283 km2: the 1065 duchy plus five cells (about 1,264 km2) on the Sussex coast, lon 0.3-0.75, lat 50.83-51.1: 'They landed at Pevensey in Sussex on 28 September and erected a wooden castle at Hastings'. The page has Norman control from Sussex to London by the end of 1066 and 'the south and east under Norman control' in 1067; Cliopatria keeps the rest of England in its Kingdom of England row to 1071 and gives it all to Norman England from 1072.

region.text: Upper Normandy, Rollo's county on the lower Seine

ledger.note: 911: the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte gives Rollo the lower Seine. Charles the Simple 'ceded the area of present-day Upper Normandy which Rollo had previously conquered'; Rollo pledged vassalage (the Duchy page adds that he agreed 'to defend them and convert to Christianity'). Cliopatria's first shape is 922; the 911 core is that shape.

region.text: Hiémois and Bessin, west to the river Vire

ledger.note: 924: Rollo's county reaches the Vire. 'Hiémois and Bessin were taken in 924'; King Radulf 'extended Rollo's county westward up to the river Vire, including the Bessin'. Cliopatria draws it in 926.

region.text: the Cotentin and a part of the Avranchin

ledger.note: 933: William Longsword is granted the Cotentin and the Avranchin. 'William Longsword in return was granted Avranchin and the heavily Norse Cotentin'; the History page: 'the Cotentin and a part of Avranchin followed in 933', 'the formerly Breton Avranchin'. Cliopatria draws it in 936; the Avranchin south of the Sélune follows in 1009-1020.

region.text: the lands of the Duchy of Normandy seized by the king, with lower Normandy given to Hugh the Great

ledger.note: 942: Louis IV takes the duchy after Longsword's murder (bridging a silence). 'Richard was about ten years old when his father was killed on 17 December 942'; Louis installed him, then 'the king reneged and seized the lands of the Duchy of Normandy' and 'split up the duchy, giving its lands in lower Normandy to Hugh the Great'. The page dates none of the seizure, so 942 is a placeholder.

region.text: the duchy returned to Richard I

ledger.note: 946: Louis IV is captured and Normandy is returned. 'In 946, at the age of 14, Richard allied himself with the Norman and Viking leaders in France. A battle was fought after which Louis IV was captured'; 'Hostages were taken and held until King Louis recognised Richard as duke, returning Normandy to him'. The combined armies of Otto, Arnulf and Louis were 'driven from the gates of Rouen' in 947.

region.text: the land between the Sélune and the Couesnon, with Mont-Saint-Michel

ledger.note: 1020: the Avranchin is completed. 'Between 1009 and 1020 the Normans took all the land between the rivers Sélune and Couesnon, including Mont Saint-Michel, and completed the conquest of Avranchin'; the decisive date is the page's upper bound. Cliopatria already holds the strip in 936.

1049: William besieges Alençon. 'William, Duke of Normandy, besieged Alençon' in 1049-1051, the town having 'risen in support of the Count of Anjou' together with Domfront and Bellême; Alençon surrendered after William had captives' hands and feet cut off and Domfront surrendered after hearing of it.
1050: the campaigns end. 'William the Conqueror completed these campaigns in 1050 by taking Passais'; the Alençon page's window is 1049-1051, without a separate date for Domfront.

1050: William takes Passais. 'William the Conqueror completed these campaigns in 1050 by taking Passais'. The History page names no former holder; the Alençon page has 'Domfront was then in Maine', so Maine is the counterpart (confidence 1, a reading of the second page). The Geoffrey II, Count of Anjou page (opened for the county-of-anjou dossier) says Geoffrey Martel 'seized the towns of Domfront and Alençon' and that William besieged Domfront through the winter of 1052, so Anjou may be the better counterpart and 1052 the better year; the reviewer should weigh the two.

region.text: England, from the Sussex coast to London and then the west and north

ledger.note: 1066: William lands in England. 'They landed at Pevensey in Sussex on 28 September and erected a wooden castle at Hastings', a few days after Stamford Bridge; the zone is the Kingdom of England, resisting until early 1071.

region.text: the Sussex coast around Pevensey and Hastings, by Cliopatria's drawing

ledger.note: 1066: Hastings. 'The battle began at about 9 am on 14 October 1066 and lasted all day... William's force defeated Harold, who was killed in the engagement, and William became king'; he was 'crowned by Ealdred on 25 December 1066, in Westminster Abbey'. Cliopatria draws a bridgehead of five cells on the Sussex coast for 1066-1071, the rest of England staying in its own row.

1071: English resistance ends at Ely. 'Early in 1071 there was a final outbreak of rebel activity in the area'; the Normans 'stormed the island, marking the effective end of English resistance'. Edwin was killed and Morcar imprisoned.

region.text: Normandy and the Sussex bridgehead, absorbed in the Anglo-Norman realm

ledger.note: 1071: the duchy passes into Norman England. After 1072 'William spent more than 75 per cent of his time in France rather than England' and he and his successors were 'largely absentee rulers' to 1204; the Duchy page keeps the dukes 'usually also kings of England' to 1204 (infobox 'Personal union with the Kingdom of England (1066-1290)'). Cliopatria hands continental Normandy to Norman England in 1072, after the Treaty of Abernethy.

wars.name: Norman conquest of England
wars.outcome: Norman victory at Hastings on 14 October 1066, William crowned 25 December 1066, and the last English resistance ended at Ely in early 1071; the Treaty of Abernethy followed in 1072.
wars.note: The page has no dated map; Cliopatria's Normandy shape holds only the Sussex coast.

wars.name: Louis IV's war with Richard I of Normandy
wars.outcome: Louis IV seized the duchy, gave lower Normandy to Hugh the Great, was captured in 946 and recognised Richard as duke; Otto, Arnulf and Louis were driven from Rouen's gates in 947.
wars.note: Not a Wikipedia article title; the page dates only 17 December 942, 946 and 947. Theobald I of Blois's attempt on Rouen in 962 was routed before it crossed the Seine.

wars.name: Norman siege of Alençon and Domfront
wars.outcome: Alençon and Domfront surrendered to William; the History page has Passais taken in 1050.
wars.note: Not a Wikipedia article title; the Alençon page gives the window 1049-1051.

certainty.note: No page opened gives a surveyed or treaty frontier for Normandy (the 911 treaty gives 'the area of present-day Upper Normandy'); the marches with Maine and Brittany shift by county. The Couesnon with Brittany is a river line only from 1009-1020.

notes: Pages: 5 of 5 budgeted. Cliopatria rows: 922-1071 is a 5-shape row. (1) No row for 911-921: new keyframe _911 carries the 922 shape. (2) Two cells are drawn too early: Mont-Saint-Michel's strip (page 1009-1020) and Passais/Domfront (page 1050); both are removed in the corrected 936 and 990 shapes and restored by ledger gains. (3) The 990 shape grows south to lat 47.99 (Alençon, Bellême, Mortagne cells) and no page opened dates it; the Alençon page calls Alençon a 10th-century buffer state and Bellême a fief held of the king, so these cells are unverified. (4) The 1066-1071 shape is a five-cell Hastings bridgehead; the rest of England stays in the Kingdom of England row until Norman England (eu-11) starts in 1072, whose shape includes Normandy. End: the dossier stops at 1071 where Cliopatria hands continental Normandy to Norman England; the pages keep the duchy a distinct fief of the French crown to 1204 (Philip II) and 1259 (Treaty of Paris), with the dukes usually kings of England; the Norman England and Angevin Empire dossiers (eu-11) and the Kingdom of France dossier (eu-10) must carry Normandy 1072-1204 and the 1204 conquest. Not done: rulers (the page lists Rollo 911-927, Longsword to 942, Richard I 942-996, William 1035-1087 but not Richard II, Richard III or Robert I); the ducal title ('between 987 and 1006' for Richard II); the Vexin and Évreux (not on the pages opened); the Channel Islands; the 1087 split, Tinchebray (1106) and Geoffrey of Anjou's conquest (the Duchy page lists his 1144-1150 rule without describing it) are after this dossier's end. The occupation of 942-946 is a bridging reading. Discrepancy: the Geoffrey II page puts the Domfront siege in winter 1052 and the county-of-anjou dossier ends its Alençon-Domfront contest in 1052, while this dossier ends it in 1050 on the History of Normandy page. Counterparts: county-of-maine, county-of-anjou, kingdom-of-brittany, kingdom-of-england, norman-england, west-franks exist or are in other groups. Region names are Natural Earth departments (Calvados, Manche, Orne) and coordinates; the gazetteer lacks Domfront, Alençon, Bellême, Mont-Saint-Michel as places, hence the coordinate radii.
